items.title: Around 50,000 Huguenots fled to England in the 1680s
items.claim: Why did French Huguenots come to England?

options.text: They were invited as agricultural labour by William III
Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes (1598) in 1685, removing Protestant rights — around 50,000 fled to England, with major settlements in Spitalfields, Soho and Canterbury
They were exiled by James II for Jacobite sympathies
Famine in Brittany drove migration in the 1680s

items.reveal:
The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (October 1685) made Protestant worship illegal in France. Perhaps 200,000-400,000 Huguenots fled total — to England, the Dutch Republic, Brandenburg, the Cape and the American colonies.

In England they brought silk-weaving (Spitalfields), gunmaking, watchmaking, banking (the Courtauld and Bosanquet families). 'Refugee' as an English word enters the language from the Huguenot experience.

Charles II had already extended denizenship to French Protestants in 1681. Anti-Catholic sentiment made absorption relatively smooth.
items.why: Migration history in Britain is much older than the 20th century. The Huguenot case is the classic example of refugees whose skills shaped an industrial sector — and whose absorption was made easier by religious alignment.

items.title: Keynes resigned from the British delegation over Versailles
items.claim: What was Keynes's role at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference?

options.text: He helped draft the reparations clauses
He was a British Treasury official; he resigned in June 1919 in protest and published 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace' in December — arguing reparations would devastate Germany and Europe
He was not present at the conference
He represented Lloyd George as foreign affairs adviser

items.reveal:
Keynes was deputy to the British Treasury delegation. His book (December 1919) accused the Big Four — especially Clemenceau and Wilson — of imposing a 'Carthaginian peace' that would ensure future conflict.

The book sold over 100,000 copies and shaped Anglo-American opinion. It helped frame the 1930s 'appeasement' logic — Germany had been wronged at Versailles and deserved revision. Historians (notably Margaret MacMillan, 'Peacemakers' 2001) have argued Keynes overstated reparations' impact: Germany paid only a fraction.

Reparations were formally cancelled in 1932 (Lausanne).
items.why: Keynes's pamphlet is itself a historical event. It shaped the inter-war policy world more than the treaty article it attacked — a reminder that narratives of treaties can matter more than treaty texts.

items.title: Mary I burned around 280 Protestants
items.claim: Mary I's reign (1553-1558) earned the 'Bloody Mary' epithet through executions. How many died?

options.text: Around 10,000 — comparable to Henry VIII's executions
Around 280 Protestants burned at the stake, plus 30 who died in prison — a smaller toll than Henry VIII's or Elizabeth I's overall execution numbers
Over 50,000 in a state campaign of terror
No confirmed executions for religion — the epithet is entirely myth

items.reveal:
John Foxe's 'Actes and Monuments' (1563, later 'Foxe's Book of Martyrs') chronicled the Marian burnings in vivid detail and became a foundational Protestant text. Henry VIII executed an estimated 57,000 (Holinshed's figure, contested) including thousands of vagrants; Elizabeth I executed around 200 Catholic priests and Jesuits.

Mary's numbers were lower in absolute terms but concentrated (1555-1558) and ideological. The propaganda effect outlasted the regime.
items.why: Reputation is unevenly distributed. Mary's image as uniquely cruel says more about the durability of Protestant propaganda than about Tudor execution rates.
